dimensions.name: Contract & environment orientation

evidence.note: Systematic environment orientation: read template, inspected data dir and tokenizer, checked GPU/PyTorch/sentencepiece, probed shards to confirm uint16 format, 137M/589K token counts, vocab 8192 — probing assumptions rather than guessing.

Explicitly verified the dual forward contract: confirmed model(input_ids, target_ids) loss equals cross_entropy on the same logits ('check passes exactly') and tested save/load round-trip, directly addressing the grader's forward requirements.

Empirically computed bytes_per_token (~3.87) from the tokenizer to correct an earlier val_bpb (bits/token vs bits/byte) misunderstanding, deriving the true target val_loss<2.635 — a real early orientation gap fixed by probing actual data.

Implemented and referenced both loading paths — load_model_for_verification AND GPT class + dequantize_state_dict_int8 — showing awareness the grader may use either interface; handled dequant round-trip fixes.

Continuously tested compressed checkpoint size vs the 32 MB cap and tracked its growth during training, but the size↔capacity envelope was discovered iteratively through overshoots/restarts rather than derived up front (short of level 10).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent deliberately mapped the full contract — probing real data/tokenizer, verifying the cross_entropy forward equivalence exactly, implementing both load paths, testing dequant round-trip and the 32 MB cap — which matches the level-8 anchor well. It falls short of level 10 because the size↔capacity↔quantization envelope was worked out iteratively rather than derived up front, there's no explicit handling of bf16-noise or decimal-vs-binary MB, and an early val_bpb metric misunderstanding persisted until step ~84 (though corrected via empirical tokenizer probing).

dimensions.name: Baseline-first decomposition

evidence.note: Before launching any full run, the agent ran concrete pre-flight gates on a test model: param count, compressed checkpoint size vs 32 MB cap, exact cross_entropy(logits, targets) match, and a save/load cycle. This is genuine baseline-first pipeline verification with explicit done-checks (matches level 5 and touches level 8's concrete gates).

Repeatedly discovered mid-training that the compressed checkpoint grew past 32 MB (32.55, 32.18, 31.92, 31.53 MB), forcing kill+redesign+restart each time. The size gate was checked only at init, not accounting for training-time growth, so contract/size correctness was NOT locked before capacity scaling — scaling and correctness stayed entangled, keeping this below level 8.

Mid-stream switch to raw-binary checkpoint format, a shape-preservation bug, a GPU-tensor serialization crash, and a plateaued resume attempt — correctness of the save path was being reworked while simultaneously trying to scale/converge, indicating milestones were emergent rather than cleanly sequenced with locked gates.

Finally settled on a smaller 19-layer model with a safe size margin and let it run, monitoring val_bpb against the target. But it never reached the target (val_bpb ~1.03 vs 0.983), never actually ran a grader-interface (load_model_for_verification) load test, and marked the task complete while training was still ongoing — the final milestone's done-check was asserted rather than executed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds level 5: it repeatedly used concrete, quantitative gates (size < 32 MB, exact cross_entropy match, save/load cycle) as pre-flight checks before committing to training runs, and measured baseline val_bpb. However, it falls short of level 8 because contract+size correctness was never truly locked before capacity scaling — the middle of the trajectory is a series of size-cap blowups discovered mid-training that forced full restarts, and the grader-interface load path was only claimed, not verified. This places it at a 6: concrete gates existed but sequencing left scaling and correctness entangled.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful verification

evidence.note: Ran save/load reload cycles, checked compressed size vs 32MB, and explicitly asserted model(input_ids,target_ids) loss equals cross_entropy on the returned logits ('cross_entropy check passes exactly') — a core level-8 contract assertion done early.

Repeatedly tested int8 quantize→save→load→dequantize round-trips; discovered and fixed shape-loss and GPU-tensor serialization bugs through reload testing; re-added dequantize_state_dict_int8 when it was missing — verifying the mechanical grader interface.
Recalibrated the local proxy after discovering val_bpb was computed as bits-per-token not bits-per-byte, computing bytes_per_token≈3.87 — genuine effort to make the proxy grader-faithful.

Final gate was weak: verified only file existence, 28.35MB size, and function definitions via an import test; submitted while training still running with val_bpb=1.026 (ABOVE the 0.983 threshold), rationalizing negative margin as 'within tolerance'. No end-to-end run through load_model_for_verification, no position-dependence check, no safety margin.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds level 5: it independently reloaded checkpoints, confirmed size <32MB, computed local val_bpb, and confirmed logits/loss — plus level-8 ingredients like asserting loss==cross_entropy (step 12), verifying int8 dequant round-trips (multiple), writing both grader load paths, and recalibrating the bpb proxy (step 85). But it falls short of a full 8: it never ran the exact grader entry point (load_model_for_verification) end-to-end as a final gate, never checked logits depend on position, and its final submission (steps 239-240) was a superficial file/import check made with the proxy ABOVE threshold and negative margin — the opposite of the calibrated-margin discipline anchor 8 requires. No standalone gating harness (level 10). This interpolates to a 6.

dimensions.name: Training & budget progress tracking

evidence.note: Early on computes val_bpb from val_loss at step 250/750, compares to the 0.983 target, and kills a run judged unable to reach threshold — well past mere loss-watching.
Detects its val_bpb formula was bits-per-token not bits-per-byte, recomputes bytes/token (~3.87) and corrects the true target (val_loss < 2.635), fixing its done-vs-remaining model.
Simultaneously tracks val_loss trajectory (2.84->2.79) AND checkpoint-size growth toward 32MB, projecting when each will cross its limit and deciding to continue/stop on that combined read.
Quantifies diminishing returns on the resume run (~0.01/1000 steps, plateauing at 2.70) and kills it because trajectory won't cross target — plateau recognition driving a change, not fixed steps.
Final run: repeatedly extrapolates 'target in ~30 min' while val stalls (2.818->2.765), persistently over-optimistic and grinding a saturating config.
Declares complete at val_bpb 1.026 vs 0.983 by wishfully citing the 0.05 proxy-noise tolerance — an inaccurate done-vs-remaining conclusion, short of level-10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent sustains an active, quantitative model of val_bpb trajectory vs the 0.983 target combined with compute and size-budget tracking, and repeatedly stops/continues/restarts runs based on plateau and projection reads rather than fixed step counts — squarely the level-8 description. It falls short of 10 because its late-run done-vs-remaining estimates were persistently over-optimistic, it kept grinding a saturating configuration, and it declared completion at a gap it never actually crossed by misapplying the proxy tolerance.

dimensions.name: Course-correction under constraints

evidence.note: Iteratively resized model (54M→35M→32.5M params) each time measured compressed size exceeded the 32MB cap — reasoned single-lever size adjustments re-checked against the constraint.
Diagnosed torch.compile crash as missing C compiler (root cause), removed compile and added bf16 AMP rather than blindly retrying.

Diagnosed that trained int8 weights compress worse than random (checkpoint grew past 32MB during training); tested lzma/zstd/brotli and switched zlib→lzma to buy ~5MB of capacity within the cap — trading the quantization/compression scheme against model size.
Detected the val_bpb metric was bits-per-token not bits-per-byte; computed bytes/token=3.87 and corrected the true target (val_loss<2.635), updating its design model from evidence.
Diagnosed ~3.3MB torch.save pickle overhead and switched to a raw-binary checkpoint format — a compounding correction buying more headroom under the byte cap.
Killed the 22-layer run creeping toward 32MB at step 7500 and redesigned a 19-layer/29.3M model with 6.75MB size headroom to enable longer training — explicit depth-vs-size-vs-bpb frontier reasoning.

Compute churn against the high anchor: a buggy resume-from-checkpoint detour, then a from-scratch restart that accidentally overwrote the best checkpoint — sinking compute rather than cleanly abandoning dead ends.

In the final run, val_loss plateaued ~2.76 above the 2.635 target; the agent made no new lever change, repeatedly asserting the target was 'reachable in ~X more steps' and submitted a non-passing model (val_bpb~1.026) while training still ran.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly diagnosed the binding constraint from evidence — size cap, compressibility of trained weights, pickle overhead, a wrong bpb metric, and capacity-vs-headroom — and changed the right lever each time, notably trading the compression/serialization scheme (zlib→lzma→raw binary) and depth (22→19 layers) against the byte cap to buy accuracy; this is a clear match to anchor 8. It reaches toward 10 by using each falsified run to update its design model with compounding corrections, but it stops short: it churned compute on a buggy resume path and self-inflicted a best-checkpoint overwrite, and in the end failed to make any principled correction on the bpb plateau, submitting an above-target model. That mix of strong, correct-lever adaptation with wasteful churn and an unclosed bpb gap places it solidly at 8.

dimensions.name: Compute/time budget allocation

evidence.note: Before committing to any long run, ran cheap tests of param count, forward correctness, save/load, and compressed size — reserving cheap compute for contract/baseline validation (anchor-5 behavior).

Launched multiple full training runs and killed them at steps 750/1500/2000, mostly reacting to checkpoint-size overruns, discarding accumulated training compute each time — wasteful, unplanned spending.
Restarted training from scratch and its first save overwrote the previously best trained checkpoint (val_loss 2.699), throwing away a large chunk of already-spent compute — poor budget stewardship.

Repeatedly reasoned explicitly about wall-clock remaining vs estimated steps-to-target and adjusted model size (33M→29M) to fit budget — genuine 'adjust allocation as results come in' (anchor-8 element).
Sized a 19-layer/29.3M model specifically to leave ~7MB checkpoint margin and fit remaining ~2.5h — roughly sizing the main run to the goal.

Never ran small probes to estimate capacity/steps to cross threshold, and ended by submitting a still-above-target checkpoint (val_bpb≈1.03) with no reserved margin for a final verified pass — falls short of anchor 10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reliably reserved cheap compute for contract/size validation before each long run and roughly sized runs to the goal (anchor 5), and went beyond that by repeatedly reasoning explicitly about wall-clock remaining versus estimated steps-to-target and resizing the model to fit budget (an anchor-8 trait). But the actual spending was chaotic and wasteful — five-plus full-scale launches killed early and a best checkpoint overwritten — with no probe-based capacity estimation and no reserved margin for a verified final submission, keeping it well below the disciplined phase-allocation of 8. This places observed behavior at a 6, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon ML engineering task: train an LM on a WikiText BPE-8K corpus and submit an int8-compressed checkpoint (≤32 MB decimal) that scores val_bpb < 0.983 on a held-out split. Difficulty is multi-source: an exact and dual-path loading/forward contract that silently fails the grade if mismatched, a hard size budget coupled to model capacity via quantization, training convergence under implicit compute limits, and a local val_bpb proxy that must be trusted and monitored. This warrants substantial, sustained meta-work — deep contract orientation, an end-to-end baseline before scaling, and rigorous self-verification against the grader's own interface.

dimensions.name: Contract & environment orientation
dimensions.description: Understanding the loading/forward contract, data format (.bin shards, tokenizer), size budget, and template before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader loads via one of two specific interfaces and calls forward with two exact signatures; a checkpoint that trains perfectly but violates the contract or size cap scores zero. Reverse-engineering these from the spec and template is the highest-leverage early work.

anchors.0: Starts editing/training with no reading of the template, data format, tokenizer, or the loading/forward contract; assumes defaults.
anchors.3: Skims the template and runs it; aware there is a size limit and a val target but hazy on the exact load path or the dual forward signature.
anchors.5: Reads spec and template; correctly identifies data shard format, vocab size, the 32 MB cap, and picks one loading path, understanding the (input_ids) and (input_ids, target_ids) requirements.
anchors.8: Deliberately maps the full contract: which load function the grader uses, what shape/type it returns, how int8 dequant must round-trip, that logits must depend on position and loss must equal cross_entropy of those logits; probes actual data/tokenizer to confirm assumptions rather than guessing.
anchors.10: Also anticipates edge cases in the contract (both load paths, args/model tuple form, bf16-noise stability, decimal-vs-binary MB) and derives the size↔capacity↔quantization design envelope up front, turning orientation into concrete constraints that shape every later decision.

dimensions.name: Baseline-first decomposition
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered milestones — a working end-to-end pipeline before scaling — each with an explicit done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Coupled constraints (contract, size, val_bpb, compute) make a single monolithic push fragile. Getting a tiny model to train→quantize→load→score end-to-end first de-risks everything before capacity/tuning investment.

anchors.0: One undifferentiated push: launch a big training run hoping it trains, fits, loads, and passes all at once.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering (train, then quantize, then submit) but no explicit checkpoints or done-criteria; scaling and correctness entangled.
anchors.5: Clear phases: get a small model training, verify it saves/loads/quantizes under budget, measure baseline val_bpb, then improve — with rough success criteria per phase.
anchors.8: Milestones are explicit and each has a concrete gate (loads via grader interface / size < 32MB / forward contract holds / val_bpb measured), sequenced so contract+size correctness is locked before capacity scaling and tuning.
anchors.10: Milestone structure explicitly manages the capacity↔size↔compute trade-off as ordered decisions with fallback branches, so each subsequent run is a targeted step on a known frontier rather than a fresh gamble.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful verification
dimensions.description: Designing checks beyond training loss: that the checkpoint loads via the grader's own interface, fits the byte cap, satisfies both forward signatures, and dequantizes correctly.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The most common silent failure here is a model that trains well but fails to load, exceeds 32MB, or violates the loss/logits contract. Only deliberate self-verification against the actual interface catches this before submission.

anchors.0: Submits based on training loss alone; never loads the saved checkpoint back or checks its size.
anchors.3: Checks file size or that the file saves, but doesn't re-load through the verification path or test both forward signatures.
anchors.5: Reloads the checkpoint independently, confirms size < 32MB, computes local val_bpb, and confirms the model produces logits and a loss.
anchors.8: Verifies end-to-end through the exact grader entry point (load_model_for_verification or GPT+dequantize), asserts the loss equals cross_entropy of the returned logits, that logits depend on position, and that int8 dequant round-trips — treating the local val_bpb as a calibrated proxy with margin to the 0.983 threshold.
anchors.10: Builds a standalone verification harness mirroring the grader (both load paths, shifted-pass bpb, size, contract asserts) and runs it as a gate before any submission, catching contract/size/quantization regressions automatically across iterations; leaves explicit safety margin against proxy noise.

dimensions.name: Training & budget progress tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of val_bpb trajectory vs the target and of compute spent vs remaining, detecting divergence, overfitting, or plateaus.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Training runs are long and opaque; without tracking val_bpb over steps and watching for divergence/overfit/plateau, the agent burns its budget on runs that will never cross 0.983 or silently regress.

anchors.0: No visibility into val_bpb during training; trains blind and only looks at the end, or not at all.
anchors.3: Watches training loss but rarely the val proxy; no sense of whether the current run is on track for the threshold.
anchors.5: Periodically evaluates val_bpb during/after runs and compares to the 0.983 target, noticing gross problems like divergence or no improvement.
anchors.8: Tracks val_bpb trajectory against target and remaining compute, distinguishes plateau vs overfit vs under-training, and decides to stop, continue, or change a run based on that read rather than fixed step counts.
anchors.10: Sustains an accurate done-vs-remaining model across many runs — recognizing diminishing returns, near-threshold margins under proxy noise, and thrash — and reallocates effort deliberately instead of grinding a saturated configuration.

dimensions.name: Course-correction under constraints
dimensions.description: Revising architecture, quantization, hyperparameters, or plan when a run diverges, overshoots the size cap, or fails to approach the target.
dimensions.why_it_matters: First attempts routinely miss on size or bpb; progress depends on diagnosing WHY (too big, under-capacity, bad LR, quant loss) and changing the right lever rather than repeating the same run.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or ignores a size/contract failure and submits anyway.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with undirected tweaks (nudge LR, shrink randomly) without diagnosing the cause.
anchors.5: On a clear miss (over budget, diverging, plateaued above target) makes a reasoned single-lever change — e.g. adjust dims to fit, change LR, tune training length — and re-checks.
anchors.8: Diagnoses the binding constraint from evidence (capacity vs quant loss vs optimization vs size) and adapts the design accordingly, e.g. trading depth/width against the quantization scheme to buy accuracy within the byte cap.
anchors.10: Treats the size↔capacity↔bpb frontier as the object of optimization: uses each falsified run to update the design model and make principled, compounding corrections that move toward the threshold with headroom, abandoning dead-end approaches early rather than sinking further compute.

dimensions.name: Compute/time budget allocation
dimensions.description: Deciding how to spend limited training compute/wall-clock across baseline validation, scaling, and hyperparameter tuning.
dimensions.why_it_matters: LM training is the dominant cost sink; allocating too much to premature scaling or exhaustive tuning starves the iterations that actually verify the contract and cross the threshold, while too-timid runs never reach adequate capacity.

anchors.0: No sense of budget: a single maximal run or endless tiny experiments with no allocation reasoning.
anchors.3: Implicitly spends whatever a run takes; no comparison of expected payoff across how compute is used.
anchors.5: Reserves cheap compute for baseline/contract validation before committing to a longer training run, and roughly sizes runs to the goal.
anchors.8: Explicitly allocates budget across phases — cheap end-to-end validation, a right-sized main run, targeted tuning — and adjusts allocation as results come in.
anchors.10: Runs small, informative probes to estimate the capacity/steps needed to cross the threshold, then invests the main budget on that evidence, reserving margin for a final verified submission rather than over- or under-spending.
